relationship: lament over apparent divine delay amid oppression
rationale: Habakkuk asks how long he must cry while wronged without being heard or saved. The psalm likewise repeatedly asks how long the Lord will turn away, then asks Him to hear lest the enemy prevail. Both voice distressed waiting for divine help.
source_text: How long, Lord, shall I cry and Thou wilt not listen? I shall cry to Thee while being wronged, and Thou wilt not save?

target_units.text: How long, Lord, wilt Thou forget me utterly? How long wilt Thou turn Thy face away from me?
How long shall I place counsels within my soul, pains within my heart by day? How long will my enemy be raised above me?
Look; hear me, Lord my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I fall asleep into death,
lest my enemy say, “I prevailed against him.” Those who afflict me will exult if I am shaken.

relationship: wrongdoing encountered in the place of judgment
rationale: Habakkuk complains of misery and impiety, with judgment against him and a judge who takes. Ecclesiastes likewise observes an ungodly person in the place of judgment and righteousness. Both locate wrongdoing where justice should be administered.
source_text: Why didst Thou show me toil and pain, to look upon misery and impiety? Judgment has come against me, and the judge takes.

target_units.text: Again I saw beneath the sun: in the place of judgment, the ungodly person was there; in the righteous person’s place, the ungodly person was there.

rationale: Habakkuk describes scattered law and distorted judgment while the impious oppresses the righteous. Isaiah likewise says judgment was driven backward, righteousness withdrew and the Lord was displeased at the absence of judgment. Both connect public injustice with the failure of judgment.
source_text: Therefore law has been scattered, and judgment is not brought to completion; the impious oppresses the righteous, so judgment will go forth distorted.

target_units.text: We drove judgment backward, and righteousness has withdrawn far away, for truth was consumed in their ways, and they could not go straight through.
Truth has been taken away, and they turned their mind away from understanding. The Lord saw, and it did not please Him that there was no judgment.

relationship: explicit later quotation of an unbelievable divine work
rationale: Habakkuk addresses despisers and announces a work they will not believe even when recounted. Acts explicitly warns about what the prophets spoke and repeats the address, wonder and vanishing, and the work that will not be believed. The wording directly connects the warning.
source_text: Look, you despisers, observe, marvel at wonders and vanish! For I am doing a work in your days that you will certainly not believe if someone recounts it.

target_units.text: Take care, then, lest what is spoken in the prophets come upon you:
‘Look, you scoffers, marvel and vanish, for I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe even if someone recounts it to you.’”

relationship: the Lord brings an invading nation
rationale: Habakkuk announces the Lord raising Chaldean warriors who seize dwellings not their own. Jeremiah likewise announces a distant nation brought against Israel to consume its produce and attack fortified cities. Both present the invading force within a divine announcement, without assigning Jeremiah Habakkuk's national label.
source_text: For look, I am raising up against you the Chaldean warriors, the bitter and swift nation, who traverse the breadth of the earth to possess dwellings not their own.

target_units.text: Behold, I am bringing a nation upon you from far away, house of Israel, says the Lord, a nation whose language’s sound you will not understand.
All are strong,

and they will devour your harvest and your bread, and devour your sons and daughters, and devour your sheep and calves, and devour your vineyards and fig orchards and olive groves; and with a sword they will thresh your fortified cities, in which you have trusted.

relationship: an imperial force claims authority for itself
rationale: Habakkuk describes the invaders' judgment and claim proceeding from themselves. Isaiah quotes the Assyrian ruler crediting his own strength and wisdom for seizing nations without resistance. Both expose the conqueror's self-assertion, in distinct descriptions of imperial power.
source_text: Fearsome and conspicuous are they; their judgment will come from themselves, and their claim will proceed from themselves.

target_units.text: For he said, “By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of understanding. I will remove nations’ boundaries, plunder their strength and shake inhabited cities.
I will seize the whole inhabited world in my hand like a nest, and lift it like abandoned eggs. There is no one who will escape me or contradict me.”

relationship: a distant invading nation compared to an eagle
rationale: Habakkuk describes horsemen rushing from afar and flying like an eagle eager to eat. Deuteronomy likewise announces a nation from afar coming like an eagle's swoop. The distance and predatory flight imagery connect the threats.
source_text: Their horses will leap beyond leopards and be fiercer than the wolves of Arabia. Their horsemen will ride out and rush from afar, flying like an eagle eager to eat.

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,

relationship: the gathering of large numbers of captives
rationale: Habakkuk pictures the invading force gathering captives like sand. Kings recounts Babylon's king deporting rulers, warriors and craftsmen in large stated numbers. The historical account illustrates mass deportation without equating its numerical totals with the sand comparison.
source_text: An end will come upon the impious who stand facing them in opposition, and they will gather captives like sand.

target_units.text: He deported Jerusalem, all the rulers, and the mighty in strength, taking ten thousand captives, and every craftsman and one who shuts up. None remained except the land’s poor.
He deported Joakim to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, and his eunuchs. He led the land’s powerful men into deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon,
and all the men of the force, seven thousand, and the craftsmen and those who shut up, one thousand—all mighty men who waged war. The king of Babylon brought them into deportation to Babylon.

relationship: siege works used against fortified cities
rationale: Habakkuk says the invaders mock fortresses, throw up a mound and seize them. Ezekiel's oracle names Babylon's king and describes building around Tyre, enclosing it with a palisade and weapons, and throwing down its walls. Both portray siege construction overcoming defenses.
source_text: They will revel among kings, and tyrants will be their toys; they will mock every fortress, throw up a mound and seize it.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord: I am bringing against you, Tyre, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north—he is king of kings—with horses, chariots, horsemen, and an assembly of very many nations.
He will kill your daughters in the plain with the sword, set an advance guard against you, build around you, and make a palisade and a ring of weapons around you; he will set his spears opposite you.
He will throw down your walls and your towers with his swords.

relationship: same-book recognition of strength as God's
rationale: Habakkuk 1:11 concludes that this strength belongs to the speaker's God. The final verse likewise calls the Lord God the speaker's strength. This explicit shared attribution is retained without changing 1:11's preceding spirit and propitiation wording.
source_text: Then the spirit will change and pass through and make propitiation. This strength belongs to my God.

target_units.text: The Lord God is my strength; He will set my feet toward completion and lead me onto the heights, to conquer in His song.

relationship: a hostile power appointed within divine judgment
rationale: Habakkuk addresses the Lord as having appointed the threatening figure for judgment. Isaiah likewise calls Assyria a rod of divine anger, while distinguishing the ruler's destructive intention. The connection concerns the power's assigned role, not agreement with every purpose of the invader.
source_text: Art Thou not from the beginning, Lord, my holy God? We shall certainly not die. Lord, Thou hast appointed him for judgment, and He formed me to reprove his discipline.

target_units.text: Woe to the Assyrians! The rod of My anger and wrath is in their hands.
I will send My anger against a lawless nation, and I will command My people to take spoils and plunder, trample the cities and reduce them to dust.
But he did not consider it this way and has not reckoned it this way in his soul; rather, his mind will turn aside, even to destroy not a few nations.

relationship: the difficulty of wicked prosperity beside righteous suffering
rationale: Habakkuk questions God's silence when the impious swallows the righteous. The psalm likewise places prosperous sinners beside the speaker's apparently vain righteousness and daily scourging. Both articulate the distress caused by the apparent advantage of the wicked.
source_text: Thine eye is pure, not to see evil things, and Thou wilt not be able to look upon distress. Why dost Thou look upon despisers? Wilt Thou remain silent when the impious swallows the righteous?

target_units.text: Behold, these are sinners, and they prosper; for the age they took possession of wealth.
And I said, “Then in vain I made my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent;
and I became scourged all day, and my rebuke comes in the mornings.”

rationale: Habakkuk likens people to fish without a leader, before describing their capture. Ecclesiastes likewise compares people caught by an evil time to fish in an evil net. Both use the vulnerability of fish to describe human exposure to harm.
source_text: Thou wilt make people like the fish of the sea and like creeping things with no leader.

target_units.text: For a person does not know his time: like fish caught in an evil net, and birds caught in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly.

relationship: the catching of people represented as fishing
rationale: Habakkuk depicts a whole catch hauled by hook, casting net and seines, continuing the comparison of people with fish. Jeremiah likewise describes fishermen sent to fish for the people, followed by hunters and repayment for wrongdoing. Both apply fishing to the taking of people, with distinct agents and instruments.
source_text: They hauled up an entire catch with a hook, dragged it in a casting net and gathered it in their seines; therefore they will rejoice and their heart will be glad.

target_units.text: Behold, I am sending the many fishermen, says the Lord, and they will fish for them; and after these things I will send the many hunters, and they will hunt them on every mountain and hill and from the rocks’ openings.
Because My eyes are upon all their ways, and their wrongdoings were not hidden before My eyes.
And I will repay double their injustices and sins, for which they profaned My land with the corpses of their abominations and with their lawless acts, by which they offended against My inheritance.

relationship: worship directed to material things associated with food and benefit
rationale: Habakkuk says the captors sacrifice to nets because these provide their rich food. Isaiah describes wood used for warmth and cooking, with the rest fashioned into a god and worshiped. Both expose worship directed toward material means of benefit, while the actions upon the material differ.
source_text: Therefore they will sacrifice to their seine and burn incense to their casting net, for through them they fattened their portion, and their foods are choice.

target_units.text: so that it might serve people for burning. Taking some, he warmed himself; after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. They worked the rest into gods and worship them.

Half of it they burned in fire, and after burning it they baked loaves over the pieces. Over it he roasted meat, ate, and was satisfied. Warmed, he said, ‘It is pleasant for me, for I am warm and have seen fire!’
He made the rest into a carved god and worships it and prays, saying, ‘Rescue me, for you are my god.’

relationship: same-book accusation of destructive action against nations and its consequence
rationale: Habakkuk 1:17 describes continuing to cast the net and kill nations without sparing them. The later woe charges the despoiling of many nations and bloodshed, then promises the remaining peoples will despoil the aggressor. The later accusation and reversal answer the earlier portrayal of unchecked harm.
source_text: Therefore they will cast their casting net and will not spare nations from continual killing.

target_units.text: Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: prophetic waiting represented by a watcher's station
rationale: Habakkuk stands at his watch to look for what God will speak. Isaiah likewise receives an instruction to station a watcher, who stands day and night and reports what is seen and heard from the Lord. Both use the watcher's position for attentive reception of a message.
source_text: I will stand at my watch and step onto a rock; I will look out to see what He will speak within me and what I shall answer concerning my reproof.

target_units.text: For thus the Lord said to me: “Go, station a watcher for yourself, and report whatever you see.
I saw mounted riders, two horsemen, a donkey rider and a camel rider. Listen with great attention,
and call Uriah to the Lord’s watchtower.” He said, “I stood continually by day, and at the camp I stood all night,
and behold, he himself comes, a rider of a two-horse team.” He answered and said, “Babylon has fallen, and all her statues and handmade objects were shattered to the ground.”
Hear, you who remain and suffer; hear what I heard from the Lord Sabaoth. Israel’s God announced it to us.

relationship: a prophetic message committed to a tablet
rationale: Habakkuk is commanded to write the vision clearly on a boxwood tablet for its readers. Isaiah likewise is commanded to write on a tablet and in a book so that the words endure. Both explicitly require a written record, with different stated purposes and materials.
source_text: The Lord answered me: “Write a vision clearly on a boxwood tablet, so that the one reading these things may pursue them.

target_units.text: Now then, sit and write these things on a tablet and in a book, because these things will endure for days of appointed times and for ever.
